title: 前漢書·卷六~卷七 (Hanshu, Siku Quanshu, vol. 3 of 57)
shelf_note: Siku Quanshu manuscript copy of the Hanshu with Yan Shigu's commentary and the Song Qi / Liu Ban notes; juan 6–7 (Annals of Emperor Wu and Emperor Zhao), which the four pages confirm.
structure_note: printed_repeats 28 and printed_backsteps 11 are what Siku half-leaves produce (the folio number is shared by the a/b sides of each leaf and restarts at each juan); the pages run in order through juan 6 into juan 7. 2 of 124 pages have no OCR, probably covers or blanks. Paddle reads the garbled 欽定四庫全書 margin as stray single characters (金 只 巳 元 …) and wrong <page-num> tags on every page.

book_verdict: The text is the Hanshu juan 6–7 with its commentary, read well on all four pages, and the English is careful with Yan Shigu's notes. But the garbled Siku margin title leaks into the reader view: as a row of stray characters on p.44 and, on p.107, as an invented commentary by a nonexistent 'Ciding'.
reader_summary: This is the Siku Quanshu manuscript of Ban Gu's Hanshu, juan 6–7 (Annals of Emperors Wu and Zhao), with Yan Shigu's commentary and the Song notes of Song Qi and Liu Ban. The transcription is of the right text and largely accurate, including the small double-column commentary. The English follows text and commentary closely, but you should know that the margin title sometimes comes through as stray characters, and once as an invented commentator's note, and that the odd name or construction is misread.

The transcription is of the right text with few slips. The English is faithful, but on some pages broken note tags make Yan Shigu's commentary read as part of Ban Gu's text, so a reader must check what is narrative and what is gloss.

reader_summary: This is the Siku Quanshu manuscript of the Hanshu, juan 2–5 (the annals of Emperors Hui, Wen and Jing and of Empress Lü), with Yan Shigu's commentary. The transcription is of the right text and mostly exact, and the English of the edicts and the commentary debates (on mourning dress, for example) is careful. Some pages are spoiled by the margin title turning into an invented commentator, and on one page the English invents an event (a moon eclipse) that the text does not mention.
